newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil prices soar on winter supply worries.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil prices soar on winter supply worries.

text.p: Heating oil prices soared on Wednesday to post-Gulf War highs as speculators bought heavily on concern that the United States and other big consumers are short of supplies heading into the winter.
In other markets, grain prices rose on cold weather worries and precious metals ended mostly lower amid uncertainty about the possibility of gold sales by the International Monetary Fund.
The Knight Ridder-Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 commodity futures ended at 247.12, up 1.81 points.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, October heating oil rose 2.08 cents a gallon to close at 71.77 cents, matching the post-Gulf War high set on November 8, 1991.
Prices soared after weekly U.S. supply statistics showed heating oil stocks remaining well below year-ago levels and European weather turned colder.
The American Petroleum Institute said distillate stocks, comprising heating oil and diesel fuel, rose just 303,000 barrels last week to 112 million, or 18 million below year-ago levels.
Traders had expected a buildup of stocks of about two million barrels in the week to prepare for winter. The United States is the world's largest heating oil market.
"The stocks are perceived as really low, and the build was lower than expected," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of trading company ARB Oil.
The U.S. inventory news earlier on Wednesday sent European heating oil prices to five-year highs.
October crude oil closed up 39 cents a barrel at $24.46 and October unleaded gasoline up 0.27 cent at 63.10 cents a gallon, buoyed by the speculative buying in heating oil.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, cold, wet weather fed worries that late maturing corn and soybeans in the Midwest would be damaged and planting of winter wheat would be delayed further.
November soybeans closed up 4-1/2 cents per bushel at $7.95-3/4 and December corn up 1-3/4 cents per bushel at $3.12-1/4. July 1997 wheat rose one cent at $3.89 per bushel.

"Wet and cold also will delay wheat plantings as well as delay corn harvest," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co. "The midday reports showed even more moisture than the morning reports, so it took off from there."
At the Commodity Exchange in New York, precious metals futures ended mostly lower as traders remained uncertain about possible selling of gold by producer nations and the International Monetary Fund.
December gold ended down 40 cents at $385.30 an ounce and December silver ended down 1.3 cents at $4.922. Both markets rose early in the session only to sell off later.
"We've seen this often in recent weeks, rallies just can't hold up," said Merrill Lynch senior commodities strategist Bill O'Neill.
"The strength of the dollar, equities and bond market is providing no incentive for precious metals investors, and producers are likely to sell into any further bounce," he said.

Concerns emerged about a proposed IMF gold sale plan after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin was reported in a European newspaper as saying the plan would eventually go ahead despite current opposition.
The plan to sell five million of the IMF's 104 million ounce reserve needs 85 percent approval by IMF member countries but Germany, Switzerland and some other countries remain opposed.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday repeated Germany's opposition to the plan.
